cards.conceptual_exposition:
A short-day plant (SDP) is a photoperiodic species in which the transition from vegetative shoot growth to floral initiation occurs only when the day length falls below a critical threshold (typically fewer than 11 to 13 hours of light per 24-hour cycle). However, classic physiological experiments utilizing controlled environmental chambers have conclusively established that short-day plants do not measure the hours of daylight; rather, they measure the duration of continuous, uninterrupted darkness. Consequently, a short-day plant is physiologically a 'long-night plant.' If an otherwise inductive long night is interrupted by even a brief flash of low-intensity light (a 'night break'), floral induction is completely abolished, and the plant remains vegetative.

The biological sensor driving this photoperiodic response is the phytochrome pigment system operating in conjunction with leaf circadian clock proteins. Phytochromes exist in two photo-reversible conformations: the physiologically inactive red-absorbing form (Pr, λmax = 660 nm) and the active far-red absorbing form (Pfr, λmax = 730 nm). During daylight hours, sunlight (which possesses a high red-to-far-red ratio of ~1.2) converts phytochrome predominantly into the active Pfr form. In short-day plants, Pfr acts as a molecular repressor of flowering: during daylight and through the early hours of darkness, high nuclear levels of Pfr promote the proteasomal degradation or transcriptional silencing of flowering inducers such as Heading date 3a (Hd3a) or FT homologs. As the dark period progresses past the critical night duration (typically 10 to 12 hours of unbroken darkness), Pfr either reverts spontaneously to Pr (dark reversion) or is broken down by cellular proteases. Once Pfr falls below a critical threshold, the transcriptional repression is relieved, allowing leaves to synthesize the mobile florigen protein (Hd3a/FT). Florigen travels acropetally through the phloem sieve elements to the shoot apical meristem, where it complexes with bZIP transcription factors to activate floral identity genes (such as APETALA1), committing the meristem to flower development. If a long night is interrupted by a flash of red light, Pr is instantly converted back into inhibitory Pfr, aborting florigen synthesis; crucially, if this red flash is immediately followed by a far-red flash, Pfr is converted back to Pr, neutralizing the interruption and restoring floral induction.

In Bangladeshi agriculture and horticulture, short-day photoperiodic responses govern the phenology and yield of several major seasonal crops. A quintessential horticultural example is the Country Bean or Hyacinth Bean (Lablab purpureus, locally known as Shim). Traditional Bangladeshi Shim landraces are obligate short-day plants that remain strictly vegetative during the long days of the summer and monsoon seasons, initiating floral buds only when day lengths shorten in late autumn (October–November), leading to winter pod production. Similarly, in commercial floriculture, Chrysanthemums (Chrysanthemum morifolium) and Poinsettias (Euphorbia pulcherrima) are strict short-day ornamentals grown for winter exhibitions. In field crops, traditional Aman rice landraces (such as Nizersail, BR22, and BR23) are photoperiod-sensitive short-day varieties that flower synchronously as autumn nights lengthen, ensuring ripening before winter cold sets in. For agricultural researchers, understanding critical night lengths prevents catastrophic planting errors: for instance, sowing photoperiod-sensitive jute (Corchorus spp.) too early in spring under short day lengths triggers premature flowering before the stem attains commercial fiber height, causing severe economic losses.
cards.infographic_recommendation: Tri-Panel Short-Day Photoperiodic Mechanism & Night-Break Blueprint: (1) Photoperiodic Critical Night Response: Comparison of flowering behavior under Short Day (>12h darkness -> Flowering), Long Day (<10h darkness -> Vegetative), and Long Night with a 5-minute Red Light Night Break (Aborted Flowering restored by subsequent Far-Red flash); (2) Phytochrome Molecular Gate: Diagram showing Pr-to-Pfr conversion under daylight and slow dark reversion relieved during long nights, derepressing Hd3a/FT florigen synthesis; (3) Bangladesh Crop Phenology Timeline: October/November autumn day-shortening triggering synchronous floral induction in traditional Country Bean (Shim) and Aman rice.

cards.biological_mechanism: Specialized subterranean monocotyledonous storage organ consisting of a flattened basal stem plate bearing an apical growing point enclosed by concentric fleshy scale leaves that accumulate carbohydrates (fructans) and water. Bulbing is photoperiod- and temperature-regulated; lengthening days induce leaf sheath base swelling via FT/florigen homologs.
cards.horticultural_practice: Vital for commercial winter (Rabi) and summer onion (Allium cepa) and garlic (Allium sativum) production in Faridpur, Pabna, and Rajshahi. Propagated via daughter cloves/sets or true seeds; cured after lifting to induce skin color and prevent postharvest fungal rots.
cards.exam_trap: True bulbs occur STRICTLY in monocots (Amaryllidaceae, Liliaceae); dicots do NOT produce true bulbs! Do NOT confuse bulbs with corms (solid stems) or tubers (thickened stem/root without scale leaves).
cards.key_crops: Onion (Allium cepa cvs. Taherpuri, BARI Piaj-1, BARI Piaj-4), Garlic (Allium sativum), Lily (Lilium), Tulip (Tulipa)
cards.notes: Essential winter spice commodity in Bangladesh; summer onion cultivars require polythene rain shelters.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'bulbus', from Ancient Greek βολβός ('bolbos', swollen plant bulb or edible root).
cards.synonyms: tunicate bulb, scaly bulb, geophytic bulb, true bulb
cards.see_also: corm, tuber, rhizome, basal plate, bulbil, allium cepa
cards.conceptual_exposition: A true bulb is a specialized, compact underground storage organ restricted exclusively to monocotyledonous angiosperms...
cards.infographic_recommendation: Tri-Panel Bulb Anatomy & Bulbing Mechanism

cards.biological_mechanism: Solid, swollen subterranean vertical stem axis composed of starch-rich parenchyma with distinct nodes, internodes, and papery tunics. Renewed annually: the mother corm exhausts its reserves, while assimilate from the new shoot accumulates to form a daughter corm and cormels above, anchored by contractile roots.
cards.horticultural_practice: The primary propagation unit for commercial cut-flower Gladiolus in Jashore and Savar. Also essential in edible tuber crops: Elephant Foot Yam (Olkochu) and Taro (Mukhi Kochu). Corms are cured and stored in cool, aerated sheds to break endodormancy.
cards.exam_trap: A corm is NOT a bulb! A bulb is composed mostly of fleshy scale leaves with a miniature basal plate; a corm is almost entirely solid stem tissue with thin papery tunics.
cards.key_crops: Gladiolus (Gladiolus grandiflorus), Elephant Foot Yam (Amorphophallus paeoniifolius), Taro (Colocasia esculenta)
cards.notes: Premier commercial cut-flower in Bangladesh floriculture; contractile roots maintain optimal subterranean depth.
cards.etymology: From Ancient Greek κορμός ('kormos', trunk, log, or severed stem).
cards.synonyms: solid bulb (historical), bulbo-tuber, cormous stem
cards.see_also: bulb, cormel, contractile root, tuber, rhizome, gladiolus, amorphophallus

cards.biological_mechanism: Transfer of pollen from the anther of one plant to the receptive stigma of a genetically distinct plant, enforcing allogamy and maximizing heterozygosity, genetic recombination, and hybrid vigor (heterosis) while preventing inbreeding depression. Promoted by dioecy, monoecy, dichogamy, and self-incompatibility.
cards.horticultural_practice: Essential for dioecious cucurbits in Bangladesh: Pointed Gourd (Potol) and Teasle Gourd (Kakrol). Farmers maintain a 1:10 male-to-female plant ratio and practice manual morning hand cross-pollination to ensure commercial fruit set and prevent unfertilized ovary drop.
cards.exam_trap: Cross-pollination between flowers on the same plant or same clonal variety is geitonogamy, which is genetically equivalent to self-pollination! True allogamy (xenogamy) requires genetically distinct plants.
cards.key_crops: Pointed Gourd (Trichosanthes dioica), Teasle Gourd (Momordica subangulata subsp. renigera), Papaya (Carica papaya), Brassica oleracea
cards.notes: Mandatory morning field practice in commercial Kakrol and Potol production across Jessore and Comilla.
cards.etymology: Compound from English 'cross' (via Latin 'crux') + 'pollination' (from Latin 'pollen', fine flour).
cards.synonyms: allogamy, xenogamy, outcrossing, inter-plant pollination
cards.see_also: self-pollination, self-incompatibility, dioecy, protogyny, entomophily, heterosis

cards.biological_mechanism: Grows non-parasitically anchored to a host tree (phorophyte) for physical support without extracting host sap. Adapted to canopy drought via aerial adventitious roots clad in velamen radicum, Crassulacean Acid Metabolism (CAM) photosynthesis, and pseudobulb water reserves.
cards.horticultural_practice: Cultivated in hanging slatted wooden baskets or mounted on coconut husk and charcoal media in shadehouses in Savar and Gazipur, ensuring superior root aeration and preventing moisture stagnation.
cards.exam_trap: Epiphytes are NOT parasites! They do not produce haustoria or tap host vascular tissues. Hemiepiphytes (like strangler figs) differ by eventually establishing subterranean root connections.
cards.key_crops: Fox-tail orchid (Rhynchostylis retusa), Vanda teres (Papilionanthe teres), Dendrobium nobile, Bird's Nest Fern (Asplenium nidus)
cards.notes: Indigenous flora of Sylhet and Chittagong Hill Tracts; high commercial value in urban floriculture.
cards.etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐπί ('epi', upon) + φυτόν ('phyton', plant).
cards.synonyms: air plant, epiphytic flora, bark-dweller, phorophytic epiphyte
cards.see_also: velamen, lithophyte, cam photosynthesis, aerial root, phorophyte, orchidaceae

cards.biological_mechanism: The specific physical, climatic, edaphic, and biotic environment in which a plant taxon naturally establishes and reproduces, shaping its genetic adaptations, temperature thresholds, photoperiodic sensitivities, and stress-tolerance mechanisms.
cards.horticultural_practice: Matching crops to Bangladesh's 30 Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZs): Barind tract for mango/jujube, coastal delta for halophytes, and Sylhet/CHT acidic hills for tea and wild citrus. Critical for in-situ conservation of crop wild relatives.
cards.exam_trap: Do not confuse habitat (the physical place where an organism lives) with ecological niche (the functional role and resource utilization pattern of the organism within its community).
cards.key_crops: Crop wild relatives of Mango (Mangifera sylvatica), Citrus (Citrus macroptera), Jackfruit (Artocarpus chama)
cards.notes: Essential for site selection, rootstock matching, and protected greenhouse microclimate engineering.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'habitat' (it dwells, from 'habitare', to inhabit).
cards.synonyms: natural provenance, ecological niche, native range, biotope
cards.see_also: microclimate, agro-ecological zone, ecophysiology, germplasm, in-situ conservation

cards.biological_mechanism: Adapted to grow anchored directly on rocks or within stone fissures (chasmophytes). Roots secrete organic acids (oxalic, malic, citric) that chemically dissolve mineral cations from rock faces. Employs succulence, velamen, or poikilohydric desiccation tolerance with CAM photosynthesis.
cards.horticultural_practice: Used in ornamental landscaping for alpine rock gardens (rockeries), stone water features, and vertical exterior green walls in urban centers like Dhaka and Chittagong.
cards.exam_trap: Lithophytes grow on rocks, whereas epiphytes grow on other plants. Both are non-parasitic autotrophs that rely on aerial and atmospheric nutrient scavenging.
cards.key_crops: Rupicolous orchids (Dendrobium, Paphiopedilum), Cliff ferns (Adiantum, Cheilanthes, Pyrrosia), Lithophytic aroids
cards.notes: Native to rocky escarpments in Bandarban, Jaflong, and Bichnakandi; key elements in vertical living architecture.
cards.etymology: From Ancient Greek λίθος ('lithos', stone/rock) + φυτόν ('phyton', plant).
cards.synonyms: epilithic plant, rupicolous flora, rock plant, saxicolous organism
cards.see_also: epiphyte, xerophyte, velamen, cam photosynthesis, rockery, landscape horticulture

cards.biological_mechanism: Systematic manipulation of crop genetic architecture via artificial hybridization, progeny selection, mutation induction, polyploidization, marker-assisted selection (MAS), and genomic editing to assemble superior allelic combinations for yield, quality, and stress resilience.
cards.horticultural_practice: Engine of horticultural development at BARI and BINA: generated Bacterial Wilt-resistant BARI Begun-8, salt-tolerant BARI Tomato-8, hybrid mangoes (BARI Aam-4), and transgenic Bt Brinjal.
cards.exam_trap: Plant breeding is not merely selection from wild nature; it encompasses controlled genetic recombination, breaking linkage drags, exploiting heterosis, and molecular validation across multiple environments.
cards.key_crops: Eggplant (Solanum melongena), Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), Potato (Solanum tuberosum), Mango (Mangifera indica)
cards.notes: Foundational discipline for food security, climate adaptation, and commercial export quality.
cards.etymology: From Old English 'plante' (shoot, sprout) + 'brēdan' (to nourish or produce offspring).
cards.synonyms: crop improvement, cultivar development, genetic crop enhancement, plant genetic breeding
cards.see_also: germplasm, heterosis, polygenic, polyploid, cross-pollination, marker-assisted selection

cards.biological_mechanism: Development of multiple embryos within a single fertilized ovule. Encompasses cleavage polyembryony (zygote splitting) and adventitious nucellar embryony (sporophytic apomixis where maternal nucellar cells differentiate into clonal embryos via CitRKD1 transcription factors).
cards.horticultural_practice: Crucial for uniform, virus-free Citrus rootstock production (Kagzi lime, Rangpur lime) in Bangladesh nurseries. Note: Bangladeshi and Indian mangoes (Fazli, Langra) are strictly monoembryonic and require grafting, unlike Southeast Asian polyembryonic rootstocks.
cards.exam_trap: Do NOT claim commercial Bangladeshi mango varieties are polyembryonic! Bangladeshi commercial mangoes are monoembryonic (producing a single variable sexual seedling). Commercial polyembryony is utilized in Citrus rootstocks.
cards.key_crops: Kagzi lime (Citrus aurantifolia), Rangpur lime (Citrus limonia), Mandarin (Citrus reticulata), Southeast Asian Mango (Kensington Pride)
cards.notes: Nucellar embryos crowd out the sexual zygote, yielding 100% maternal clonal rootstocks from seed.
cards.etymology: From Ancient Greek πολύς ('polys', many) + ἔμβρυον ('embryon', unhatched embryo). Coined by Leeuwenhoek in 1719.
cards.synonyms: nucellar polyembryony, adventitious polyembryony, multiple embryony
cards.see_also: apomixis, nucellar embryony, zygotic embryo, citrus, mangifera indica, rootstock

cards.biological_mechanism: Phenotypic trait controlled by the cumulative, additive action of multiple independent genes located at different quantitative trait loci (QTLs). Exhibits continuous Gaussian variation ($P = G + E + G \times E$) rather than discrete Mendelian segregation.
cards.horticultural_practice: Applied in vegetable breeding at BARI Gazipur for evaluating complex yield components, heat tolerance in summer tomato, fruit total soluble solids (°Brix), and durable horizontal disease resistance against late blight and anthracnose.
cards.exam_trap: Polygenic (horizontal) resistance is governed by many genes and is racially non-specific and durable; monogenic (vertical) resistance is governed by a single major gene and is easily broken by single pathogen mutations.
cards.key_crops: Tomato (fruit weight, °Brix, lycopene), Brinjal (yield, shoot borer tolerance), Potato (late blight horizontal resistance)
cards.notes: Requires biometrical statistics, diallel crossing, and QTL mapping across segregating populations.
cards.etymology: From Ancient Greek πολύς ('polys', many) + -γενής ('-genes', born/producing). Coined by Kenneth Mather (1940s).
cards.synonyms: quantitative, multigenic, polyfactorial, QTL-controlled
cards.see_also: quantitative trait loci, heritability, plant breeding, continuous variation, horizontal resistance

cards.biological_mechanism: Possesses three or more complete chromosome sets ($3n, 4n, 6n,$ etc.). Induces the 'gigas' effect: expanded cell size, larger stomata, darker thicker leaves, and enlarged floral and fruit organs. Triploids ($3n$) exhibit meiotic chromosome unbalance, causing gametic abortion and complete seedlessness.
cards.horticultural_practice: Essential for commercial banana cultivars in Bangladesh (Amritasagar, Sabri, Champa), which are sterile triploids ($3n=33$). Also utilized in commercial seedless watermelon ($4n \times 2n \rightarrow 3n$) and tetraploid floricultural ornamentals (colchicine-doubled marigolds and orchids).
cards.exam_trap: Do NOT claim mangoes are polyploid! Commercial mangoes are diploid ($2n=40$). Commercial horticultural polyploids are bananas (triploid), seedless watermelon (triploid), strawberries (octoploid), and daylilies (tetraploid).
cards.key_crops: Commercial Banana (Musa acuminata / M. balbisiana, 3n), Seedless Watermelon (Citrullus lanatus, 3n), Colchicine Marigold (Tagetes erecta, 4n)
cards.notes: Triploidy confers total seedlessness; tetraploidy confers the gigas morphological enlargement.
cards.etymology: From Ancient Greek πολύς ('polys', many) + -πλόος ('-ploos', -fold) + εἶδος ('eidos', form). Coined by Eduard Strasburger (1916).
cards.synonyms: polyploid cultivar, euploid, gigas plant, chromosome-doubled cultivar
cards.see_also: autopolyploid, allopolyploid, triploid, colchicine, seedless watermelon, gigas effect

cards.biological_mechanism: Heterotrophic organism that derives organic nutrition by secreting extracellular hydrolytic enzymes (cellulases, lignin peroxidases) to digest dead biopolymers, absorbing soluble simple sugars and minerals. Modern taxonomy: strictly fungi and bacteria; non-green plants are mycoheterotrophs.
cards.horticultural_practice: The biological foundation of the commercial mushroom industry in Bangladesh: Oyster mushroom (Pleurotus ostreatus) and Paddy straw mushroom (Volvariella volvacea) grown on pasteurized straw. Also drives rural vermicomposting and Trichocompost production.
cards.exam_trap: Plants are NEVER true saprophytes! Green plants are photoautotrophs (holophytes); non-photosynthetic flowering plants (Monotropa) are mycoheterotrophs that parasitize mycorrhizal fungi. True saprophytes are strictly fungi and bacteria.
cards.key_crops: Oyster mushroom (Pleurotus ostreatus), Milky mushroom (Calocybe indica), Paddy straw mushroom (Volvariella volvacea), Trichoderma harzianum
cards.notes: Converts agricultural waste (straw, sawdust, bagasse) into protein-rich human food and organic soil amendments.
cards.etymology: From Ancient Greek σαπρός ('sapros', rotten/decayed) + φυτόν ('phyton', plant).
cards.synonyms: saprotroph, saprobe, detritivore, necrotrophic decomposer
cards.see_also: fruiting body, spawn culture, olericulture, mycoheterotrophy, composting

cards.biological_mechanism: Genetically controlled pre-fertilization barrier governed by the multiallelic S-locus: rejects self-pollen to enforce allogamy. Gametophytic SI (Solanaceae/Rosaceae): pollen tube arrested in style by stylar S-RNase. Sporophytic SI (Brassicaceae): pollen arrested on stigma by SCR/SP11 binding to SRK receptor kinase.
cards.horticultural_practice: Harnessed in Brassica vegetable breeding at BARI (Cabbage, Cauliflower, Radish) to mass-produce 100% authentic F1 hybrid seeds without manual emasculation. In fruit orchards (Kul / Ziziphus mauritiana, Apple), pollinizer cultivars are interplanted to avoid complete crop failure.
cards.exam_trap: Do NOT confuse self-incompatibility (viable gametes rejected by genetic recognition) with male sterility (failure to produce viable pollen). Mango is NOT self-incompatible; commercial SI issues are in Brassicas, Kul, and Rosaceae.
cards.key_crops: Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata), Cauliflower (B. oleracea var. botrytis), Radish (Raphanus sativus), Apple (Malus domestica), Kul (Ziziphus mauritiana)
cards.notes: Essential for designing orchard pollination layouts and eliminating emasculation in F1 hybrid seed production.
cards.etymology: From English 'self' + Late Latin 'incompatibilis' (not suffering together).
cards.synonyms: SI, physiological self-sterility, genetic incompatibility, allogamy enforcer
cards.see_also: cross-pollination, self-pollination, s-locus, s-rnase, f1 hybrid seed production

cards.biological_mechanism: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of the same flower (autogamy) or another flower on the same plant (geitonogamy). Facilitated by cleistogamy, homogamy, and protective petal closures (keel petals). Increases homozygosity by 50% each generation ($1 - (1/2)^m$) without inbreeding depression.
cards.horticultural_practice: The foundation of true-to-type vegetable seed production in Bangladesh: Tomato, Brinjal, Chili, Country Bean (Shim), and Peas. Enables smallholders to save open-pollinated variety (OPV) seeds year after year without genetic segregation.
cards.exam_trap: Geitonogamy is ecologically cross-pollinated (by insects) but genetically self-pollinated! Both autogamy and geitonogamy result in identical genetic homozygosity.
cards.key_crops: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), Brinjal (Solanum melongena), Chili (Capsicum annuum), Country Bean (Lablab purpureus), Pea (Pisum sativum)
cards.notes: Enables affordable farmer-saved seed systems across rural Bangladesh without hybrid seed repurchasing.
cards.etymology: From Old English 'self' + Latin 'pollen' (fine mill flour).
cards.synonyms: autogamy, selfing, self-fertilization, idiogamy
cards.see_also: cross-pollination, cleistogamy, self-incompatibility, inbreeding, true-to-type seed

cards.biological_mechanism: Terminal, genetically programmed developmental phase (Programmed Cell Death / PCD) of orderly macromolecular dismantling and nutrient remobilization. Chloroplasts are degraded first (chlorophagy; chlorophyllase/PAO unmasking carotenoids; Rubisco digested into phloem-loaded amino acids). Accelerated by ethylene/ABA; antagonized by cytokinins.
cards.horticultural_practice: Target of postharvest shelf-life extension: cut flowers (gladiolus, rose, tuberose) in Jashore treated with silver thiosulfate (STS) or 1-MCP to block ethylene-induced petal senescence; leafy greens treated with evaporative cooling and pre-harvest cytokinin/calcium sprays.
cards.exam_trap: Senescence is NOT passive accidental death or injury necrosis! It is an active, orderly, energy-requiring programmed developmental process designed to remobilize nutrients to reproductive or storage sinks.
cards.key_crops: Cut flowers (Gladiolus, Tuberose Polianthes tuberosa, Rose), Leafy vegetables (Spinach, Red Amaranth Lalshak)
cards.notes: Controlling senescence is the central objective of cold chains, MAP packaging, and anti-ethylene postharvest handling.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'senescentia' (old age), from 'senescere' (to grow old, from 'senex').
cards.synonyms: programmed cell death (PCD), physiological aging, leaf yellowing, organ senescence
cards.see_also: abscission, ethylene, cytokinin, shelf-life, postharvest, chlorophagy, sags

cards.biological_mechanism: Duration harvested commodities remain marketable and sound. Inversely proportional to respiration rate and ethylene production. Climacteric fruit (mango, banana, tomato) exhibit autocatalytic ethylene/respiration surges; cell wall pectins are solubilized by polygalacturonase (PG), accelerating softening. Respiration doubles/triples per 10°C rise ($Q_{10}$).
cards.horticultural_practice: Critical to overcoming 25-40% postharvest losses in Bangladesh. Postharvest protocols at BARI: Hot Water Treatment (HWT at 52°C for 5 min) against anthracnose, combined with 12°C ventilated plastic crate transit, doubles commercial mango shelf-life from 6 to 14-18 days.
cards.exam_trap: Do not store tropical/subtropical fruits (mango, banana) below 10-12°C! Sub-optimal chilling induces chilling injury (pitting, uneven ripening, skin browning), ruining shelf-life.
cards.key_crops: Mango (Mangifera indica), Banana (Musa spp.), Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), Papaya (Carica papaya)
cards.notes: Preserving shelf-life without chemical adulterants (formalin) is essential for domestic food safety and export compliance.
cards.etymology: From English 'shelf' + 'life'. 20th-century commercial marketing and postharvest terminology.
cards.synonyms: storage life, postharvest longevity, marketable lifespan, keeping quality
cards.see_also: senescence, respiration rate, ethylene, climacteric, cold chain, postharvest, modified atmosphere packaging

cards.biological_mechanism: Failure to produce functional gametes or viable seeds. Cytoplasmic Male Sterility (CMS) is governed by mitochondrial mutations causing tapetal programmed cell death and pollen abortion; restored by nuclear Rf genes. Contrasts with meiotic triploid sterility ($3n$) or stress-induced pollen abortion (>35°C).
cards.horticultural_practice: The foundation of commercial F1 hybrid seed production at BARI and BRRI in Chili, Tomato, Mustard, and Rice using the CMS 3-line system (A-line sterile, B-line maintainer, R-line restorer), completely eliminating manual emasculation costs.
cards.exam_trap: Do not confuse male sterility (absolute abortion of viable pollen) with self-incompatibility (viable pollen rejected by stigmatic/stylar S-locus recognition).
cards.key_crops: Chili (Capsicum annuum), Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea), Hybrid Rice (Oryza sativa)
cards.notes: Essential biotechnological tool for hybrid seed production; temperature-induced sterility causes blossom drop in greenhouses.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'sterilitas' (barrenness, unfruitfulness, from 'sterilis').
cards.synonyms: male sterility, reproductive barrenness, gametic abortion, ovule/pollen sterility
cards.see_also: cytoplasmic male sterility, cross-pollination, hybrid seed production, meiotic arrest, f1 hybrid

cards.biological_mechanism: Swollen underground stem formed at a stolon apex bearing nodes ('eyes') with dormant axillary buds arranged spirally. Tuberization is induced by short photoperiods and cool nights triggering leaf SP6A tuberigen (FT homolog) translocation to stolon tips, driving radial cell expansion and massive starch synthesis.
cards.horticultural_practice: The potato (Solanum tuberosum) is Bangladesh's #1 horticultural food crop (>10 million tons/yr, Munshiganj and Bogura). Propagated via certified seed tubers produced from aeroponic tissue culture; stored at 2-4°C followed by diffused-light sprouting (chitting).
cards.exam_trap: A potato is a STEM tuber (has nodes, internodes, eyes); a sweet potato is a TUBEROUS ROOT (modified root, lacks eyes/nodes, sprouts adventitiously). Never conflate the two!
cards.key_crops: Potato (Solanum tuberosum cvs. Diamant, Cardinal, BARI Alu-7, Asterix), Tuberous Begonia
cards.notes: Major cash crop and staple carbohydrate source across the northern alluvial floodplains of Bangladesh.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'tuber' (a swelling, bump, or truffle). Applied in 16th-century Renaissance herbals.
cards.synonyms: stem tuber, starchy underground tuber, seed potato (production term)
cards.see_also: stolon, tuberous root, eye (bud), potato, sp6a, dormancy, tuberization

cards.biological_mechanism: Specialized multi-layered spongy epidermis of non-living, empty cells with spiral/reticulate wall thickenings covering orchid aerial roots. Capillary action absorbs rain/dew rapidly. When dry, air-filled dead cells reflect light (silvery-white); when wet, they become transparent, unmasking underlying chloroplast-rich living cortex for photosynthesis.
cards.horticultural_practice: Essential in commercial orchid nurseries (Savar, Gazipur): grown in slatted baskets with charcoal and coconut husk. Velamen color serves as the moisture indicator: irrigate when roots turn silvery-white; withhold water when translucent green to avoid root rot.
cards.exam_trap: Velamen cells themselves are DEAD at maturity and DO NOT contain chloroplasts! The green color seen in wet roots comes from the underlying living cortex visible through the transparent, water-filled dead velamen.
cards.key_crops: Fox-tail orchid (Rhynchostylis retusa), Vanda teres (Papilionanthe teres), Dendrobium nobile, Aerides odorata
cards.notes: Critical ecological adaptation of canopy epiphytes; optical indicator for watering in orchid floriculture.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'vēlāmen' (veil, covering, or mantle, from 'vēlum').
cards.synonyms: velamen radicum, aerial root mantle, epiphytic root sheath
cards.see_also: epiphyte, aerial root, exodermis, orchidaceae, crassulacean acid metabolism

cards.biological_mechanism: Environmental stress factors that are non-biological in origin, such as drought, extreme temperatures, nutrient deficiencies, and pollution, which can negatively impact plant growth, development, and productivity.
cards.horticultural_practice: In the coastal regions of Bangladesh, rice farmers are developing salt-tolerant varieties to combat the increasing abiotic stress caused by rising sea levels and soil salinity.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to drought stress, heat stress, nutrient deficiency, salinity stress. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.
cards.see_also: drought stress, heat stress, nutrient deficiency, salinity stress

cards.biological_mechanism: Biotic stress refers to the adverse effects on plant growth, development, and yield caused by living organisms such as pathogens, pests, and herbivores, mediated through direct damage, nutrient competition, or hormonal disruption.
cards.horticultural_practice: In a mango orchard, the application of fungicides and insecticides is crucial to mitigate biotic stress caused by anthracnose and mango hopper infestations, respectively.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to pathogen, pest, herbivore, plant defense mechanisms, plant-pathogen interaction. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.
cards.see_also: pathogen, pest, herbivore, plant defense mechanisms, plant-pathogen interaction

cards.biological_mechanism: A specialized subterranean geophytic storage organ consisting of a shortened, disc-shaped basal stem plate bearing an apical growing shoot primordium enclosed by concentric layers of fleshy, modified scale leaves that store carbohydrates, water, and fructans.
cards.horticultural_practice: In the commercial spice belt of Faridpur, farmers transplant onion seedlings into raised beds in November, where shortening winter days promote vigorous vegetative foliage before lengthening spring days trigger bulb swelling.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to corm, tuber, rhizome, basal plate, bulbil, allium cepa. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.
cards.see_also: corm, tuber, rhizome, basal plate, bulbil, allium cepa

cards.biological_mechanism: A solid, swollen, vertical subterranean stem axis that functions as a perennating carbohydrate storage organ, characterized by distinct nodes, internodes, and papery tunics derived from dead leaf bases, renewed annually above the shriveling parent corm.
cards.horticultural_practice: Commercial gladiolus growers in Jashore lift and cure daughter corms and cormels after floral spike harvest, storing them in aerated crates to break dormancy prior to autumn planting.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to bulb, cormel, contractile root, tuber, rhizome, gladiolus, amorphophallus. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.
cards.see_also: bulb, cormel, contractile root, tuber, rhizome, gladiolus, amorphophallus

cards.biological_mechanism: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower on one plant to the receptive stigma of a flower on a genetically distinct plant of the same or sexually compatible species, enforcing allogamy and generating heterozygous genetic combinations.
cards.horticultural_practice: In the intensive pointed gourd fields of Jessore, farmers carry male potol blossoms at dawn to hand-pollinate female flowers, ensuring complete fruit set and preventing premature ovary drop.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to self-pollination, self-incompatibility, dioecy, protogyny, entomophily, heterosis. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.

cards.biological_mechanism: The commercial propagation vehicle wherein a carrier substrate (sterilized cereal grains such as wheat, rye, or sorghum, or sawdust) is fully colonized by pure, vegetative dikaryotic mycelium of a selected mushroom strain, acting as the biological seed or inoculum for commercial substrate spawning.
cards.horticultural_practice: Sterilized wheat grain bags are inoculated with mother mycelium in a laminar airflow chamber to produce vigorous grain spawn culture for oyster mushroom (Pleurotus ostreatus) bag production.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to mother culture, mycelium, Agaricus bisporus, Pleurotus ostreatus, substrate pasteurization. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.

cards.biological_mechanism: The physiological, genetic, or cytological condition wherein a plant is incapable of producing functional, viable gametes (pollen grains or ovules) or setting viable seeds, encompassing cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS), genic sterility, and environmental sterility.
cards.horticultural_practice: Vegetable hybrid seed producers at BARI utilize Cytoplasmic Male Sterility (CMS) three-line breeding systems to mass-produce authentic F1 hybrid chili seeds without manual emasculation.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to cytoplasmic male sterility, cross-pollination, hybrid seed production, meiotic arrest, f1 hybrid. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.
cards.see_also: cytoplasmic male sterility, cross-pollination, hybrid seed production, meiotic arrest, f1 hybrid

cards.biological_mechanism: In horticultural field trials and physiological research, the planned over-allocation of experimental units, buffer plants, or guard-row specimens beyond the minimum sample size (n) required to account for destructive physiological sampling, microclimatic border gradients, or unforeseen biotic attrition without compromising statistical power.
cards.horticultural_practice: In field experiments evaluating deficit irrigation on mango cultivars, researchers planted a 15% surplus of guard-row trees to accommodate destructive leaf water potential sampling without creating artificial border canopy gaps.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to guard row, border effect, destructive sampling, statistical power, randomized complete block design. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.
cards.see_also: guard row, border effect, destructive sampling, statistical power, randomized complete block design

cards.biological_mechanism: A specialized form of vegetative propagation in which a single scion bud attached to a small shield of bark and wood (shield bud) is inserted into a T-shaped incision cut through the bark to the active vascular cambium of a rootstock.
cards.horticultural_practice: In commercial stone-fruit nurseries, propagators conduct T-budding in mid-to-late summer when the rootstock bark is actively 'slipping', facilitating rapid insertion and union of the shield bud.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to chip budding, rootstock, scion, vascular cambium, bark slipping. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.
cards.see_also: chip budding, rootstock, scion, vascular cambium, bark slipping

cards.biological_mechanism: A thickened, fleshy subterranean storage organ; in strict botanical terminology, a modified underground stem (stem tuber) formed at a stolon apex, bearing spirally arranged nodes ('eyes') with axillary buds capable of generating new clonal plants.
cards.horticultural_practice: Commercial potato growers in Munshiganj plant sprouted seed tubers of the variety 'Diamant' into raised ridges, where subterranean stolons swell into high-yielding tubers under cool winter nights.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to stolon, tuberous root, eye (bud), potato, sp6a, dormancy, tuberization. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.

cards.biological_mechanism: Describing a plant or plant part with irregular patches or stripes of different colors, typically resulting from a genetic mutation that disrupts chlorophyll production in certain cells or tissues.
cards.horticultural_practice: In Bangladesh, the variegated Anthurium andraeanum cultivar 'Red Majesty' is prized for its vibrant red spathes and contrasting white variegation on the leaves, making it a popular ornamental plant in urban gardens.
cards.exam_trap: Key distinction required: related to chlorophyll, albino, chimerism, ornamental horticulture. Be prepared to differentiate from related physiological or nursery concepts.

cards.biological_mechanism: A specialized, multi-layered epidermal sheath of non-living, air-filled cells covering the aerial adventitious roots of epiphytic orchids and aroids, functioning in rapid moisture absorption and protective insulation against canopy desiccation.
cards.horticultural_practice: Commercial orchid growers in Gazipur withhold watering when aerial roots display a translucent green hue, applying moisture only when the velamen dries to a silvery-white color to prevent root rot.
